subject: Creativity
title: Why We Laugh: The Evolution of Humor
description: Learn Why We Laugh: The Evolution of Humor in one minute.

hook.text: Rats laugh when tickled. Great apes play pranks. Laughter existed millions of years before language — it's not a human.

buildup.text: Neuroscientist Jaak Panksepp discovered that rats emit ultrasonic 'chirps' during play — the earliest known form of.

discovery.text: Laughter evolved as a social bonding signal. It says: 'We're playing, not fighting. You're safe.

twist.text: Humans laugh 30x more in groups than alone. Laughter isn't primarily about humor — it's about connection and social.

climax.text: We didn't evolve humor because it's funny. We evolved it because groups that laughed together survived together.

punchline.text: Laughter is older than language. We bonded through giggles before words.

quiz.question: What did Jaak Panksepp discover about rats?
options: They emit ultrasonic chirps (laughter) when playing

details.summary: Laughter evolved as a social bonding signal long before language. Rats chirp when tickled, great apes play pranks, and humans laugh thirty times more in groups than alone. Humor is fundamentally about connection, not comedy.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding laughter's evolutionary roots reveals why humor is essential to human relationships, group cohesion, and social survival rather than mere entertainment.
takeaways: Laughter predates human language by millions of years
Rats produce ultrasonic chirps during play resembling laughter
Humans laugh far more in social settings than alone

faq.question: Why do we laugh more in groups than alone?
faq.answer: Laughter evolved as a social signal that communicates safety and belonging. It tells others we are playing, not threatening. This bonding function means laughter is triggered far more by social context than by humor itself.

faq.question: Do animals other than humans laugh?
faq.answer: Yes. Great apes, rats, and some other mammals produce laughter-like vocalizations during play. Neuroscientist Jaak Panksepp documented ultrasonic chirps in rats that function similarly to human laughter.
